Ahmed Sohel j : This First Miscellaneous Appeal at the instance of the appellant Md Shah Alam is directed against the judgment and order dated 7-7-2013 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali, allowing the preemption Miscellaneous Case No.14 of 2011 under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949.

The pre-emptee-purchaser developed the case property by raising wall and filling earth on the case property and spent Taka 2,00,000 in raising 132 feet wall and Taka 1,00,000 in filling earth. The pre-emptee developed the case land by spending huge amount of money. The pre-emptor had knowledge at the time of giving possession of the case property The pre-emptee-purchaser by mutating the case property opened Khatian No.4161 in his name and paid off rent regularly. The preemptor with false claim filed the instant suit. Accordingly, he prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 13. He further submits that the pre-emptor is not a stranger rather he is a co-sharer in the suit land. He is in the possession of the suit property by purchase since 1968. Furthermore, the suit is not barred by the law of limitation as the pre-emptor filed the case within the statutory period of stipulated time of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act. The pre-emptor successfully proved his definite date of knowledge regarding the disputed kabala and after knowing the existence of the deed, immediately filed the pre-emption case in accordance with law. The trial Court below elaborately discussed in his judgment by scrutinizing the evidence, referring to exhibits No.1 and 1(Ka) from where, it is apparent that the pre-emption case is not barred by the law of limitation. 

 15. He finally submits that the trial Court on proper consideration of the settled principle of law arrived at a right findings that in a case of pre-emption under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, if a tenant is co-sharer in the plot he is also treated as a co-sharer in that plot even if the said plot is recorded in more than one khatian. In support of his submissions, he referred two decisions, reported in 65 DLR (AD) 82 and 7 ADC 603. Accordingly, he prayed for dismissing the Appeal and discharging the Rule.

 28. On a close scrutiny of the evidence on record along with exhibits, it appears that admittedly the pre-emptor owns a portion of land in SA plot No.1848. There is nothing on record to show that this plot was partitioned by metes and bounds between the parties. The case land is situated in the Municipal area as such section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act is attracted in the present case not section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 29. Now, for better understanding let us examine section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, which is as follows:— 

 "It is evident that this section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act does not say about the right of pre-emption of co-sharers of a holding but it says about the right of pre-emption of the sharers of the land. "Land" means land. 'Land' does not mean 'holding' or 'tenancy'. Land can be divided by partition, 'holding can be divided by separation of joma'. After partition of any land by metes and bounds a co-sharer remains no more co-sharer of the land and loses all his right, title and interest in that land save and except his own share only even if the original holding/tenancy remains intact and there is no division or separation of tenancy. Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act has given the right of pre-emption to the co-sharer tenants of the non-agricultural land while section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has given the right of pre-emption to the co-sharer tenants of the holding. To seek pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act the petitioner does not require to be co-sharer of the holding, but he requires to be co-sharer of the land. The High Court Division, obviously, has failed to take into consideration the distinction between land and holding." 

 34. In the case of SM Basiruddin vs Z Islam, reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230, it has been held that 'the expression non agricultural land' used in section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act is not synonymous with the word ' holding` as used in the 'Bengal Tenancy Act or State Acquisition of Tenancy Act.' 

 35. From the above discussions, it is clear that in a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, the question of co-sharership in the holding or tenancy is immaterial, the question of co-sharership in the 'land' is material i.e. under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, the pre-emptor does not require to be co-sharer of the holding, but requires to be co-sharer of the land. 

 36. In the above facts and circumstances of the case, it is apparent that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the land transferred and as such entitled to get pre-emption of this land under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Ad.

Although, the trial Court had considered the issue of development cost in the impugned judgment, however, there is no doubt from the evidence on record that the Pre-emptee-Appellant has spent money for the development of the case land and accordingly, as per section 24 (3) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, the Appellant is entitled to get the development cost.
